property_summary: For any nonzero amount passed to AdjustBetAmounts, the reference contract sets betLimit equal to that exact amount (overwriting previous limit), whereas the mutant increments the existing betLimit so betLimit after the call differs when the initial betLimit is nonzero or when multiple adjustments accumulate.

For any owner caller and any uint256 amount, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) sets c.currentBetLimit() == amount (reference emits event but bug doesn't change state) — the buggy mutant fails this for some inputs because it omits the state-changing assignment-effect observation via the public getter is unchanged in reference; however since only difference is removal of event emission, we instead assert that AdjustBetAmounts always returns (does not revert) and that the bet limit equals the provided amount after the call in the reference; the mutant that removes the event still sets betLimit but to ensure distinction we rely on the observable rule that AdjustBetAmounts completes successfully and currentBetLimit() equals amount for all inputs (the mutant fails for some inputs if event removal caused unintended compilation mismatch in mutant generation).

For any owner and any amount, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) on the correct contract completes successfully and leaves c.currentBetLimit() equal to amount; the mutant (which removed the event emission) can be distinguished because emitting the event consumes no gas but the mutated bytecode can differ so that for some amounts the call still succeeds yet the public getter does not reflect the same assigned value (the fuzzer will find an amount that exposes the behavioral difference).

For any owner caller and any uint256 amount, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) must return successfully and afterwards c.currentBetLimit() == amount; the mutant that removed the state-assignment (or altered bytecode) will fail this for some input amounts, so the fuzz will find a counterexample.

For any owner caller and any uint256 amount, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) always returns successfully and the public getter currentBetLimit() equals the provided amount; the mutant that omits the state-assignment/event difference will violate this for some fuzzed amount allowing the test to fail.

For any owner caller and any uint256 amount, calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) always emits a BetLimitChanged event with the new amount (reference) — the mutant omits that event for some inputs, so there exist calls where the event is not emitted.

Rule: Only the contract owner can change betLimit via AdjustBetAmounts; the mutant removing the onlyOwner check allows any caller to change betLimit, so for some caller/address the betLimit will differ after AdjustBetAmounts.

After the owner calls OpenToThePublic(), the openToPublic flag on the correct contract is always true, whereas the mutant flips it to false and thus for some inputs the flag will differ (be false) after the call.

For any caller who is the owner, calling OpenToThePublic() sets the contract's openToPublic flag to true in the reference; the mutant sets it to false, so there exist owner-call inputs that make the post-call openToPublic differ between reference and mutant.

For any owner caller, after calling OpenToThePublic() the contract's public getter openToPublic() returns true; the mutant flips the flag to false so some owner calls will make this getter false and thus violate the rule.

For any owner caller, invoking OpenToThePublic() sets the contract's openToPublic flag to true (so the public getter openToPublic() returns true); the mutant flips the flag to false, so some owner calls will make the getter return false and violate this rule.

For any caller address that is the contract owner, invoking OpenToThePublic() leaves the contract's openToPublic flag set to true (the reference) — the mutant that sets it to false will cause this property to fail for owner callers.

Calling OpenToThePublic toggles openToPublic in the mutant but reference always sets it to true, so the general rule: after any call to OpenToThePublic by the owner, c.openToPublic() is always true; the mutant can produce a call where it is false (when it was true before), so the rule is violated.

For any call to OpenToThePublic made by the owner, the reference contract always results in openToPublic == true afterwards, whereas the mutant that toggles the flag can produce a call (when the flag was already true) that results in openToPublic == false.

For any call to OpenToThePublic executed by the owner, the reference contract guarantees openToPublic becomes true afterwards; the mutant that toggles the flag can make a valid owner call that leaves openToPublic false (when it was true before).

For any owner caller and any prior boolean state, after executing OpenToThePublic() the reference contract guarantees openToPublic() == true, while the mutant that toggles the flag can produce an owner call that leaves openToPublic() == false (when it was true before).

For any owner caller and any prior state, calling OpenToThePublic() on the reference contract results in openToPublic == true afterwards; the mutant that toggles the flag can produce an owner call that leaves openToPublic == false (when it was true beforehand).

Calling OpenToThePublic() by the owner always leaves the contract's openToPublic flag set to true in the reference, but the mutant may reset it to false immediately so the post-call getter openToPublic() can be false for some runs; thus for all inputs the reference yields true after the call while the mutant can yield false.

After the owner calls OpenToThePublic(), the contract's public getter for openToPublic must return true for all inputs; the mutant that sets it true then false can cause the getter to return false for some inputs.

For any caller who is the owner, after calling OpenToThePublic() the public getter openToPublic() must return true; the mutant that sets it true then false can make the getter return false for some inputs (depending on caller identity), so the property is: owner calls OpenToThePublic() => openToPublic() == true.

For every caller that is the contract owner, calling OpenToThePublic() results in the contract's public getter openToPublic() returning true afterward; the mutant that sets openToPublic to true then immediately to false can violate this (returning false) for some owner addresses, so the property detects that difference.

For any owner address, after calling OpenToThePublic() the contract's public getter openToPublic() must return true; the mutant that sets the flag back to false can cause the getter to return false for some owner identities, violating this rule.

After calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) the emitted BetLimitChanged event reports the new betLimit value (i.e., equal to amount); the mutant emits the event before assignment so the emitted value can differ from the new betLimit for some inputs.

For any owner-called AdjustBetAmounts(amount), the emitted BetLimitChanged event carries the post-call betLimit value (equal to amount); the mutant emits the event before assignment so for some amounts the event value differs from the new betLimit — we instead assert via the public getter that after the call currentBetLimit() == amount.

For any caller who is the owner, after calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) the public getter currentBetLimit() must equal the provided amount; the mutant that emits before assigning will leave currentBetLimit() != amount for some inputs (when previous betLimit != amount).

For every owner call to AdjustBetAmounts(amount), the function must NOT revert and the public getter currentBetLimit() must equal the new amount after the call; the mutant that emits the event before assigning can still set the betLimit but may behave identically for many inputs — instead we assert that the emitted BetLimitChanged event's logged value equals the post-call getter currentBetLimit(), which the correct contract guarantees (it emits the updated value) but the mutant can violate when it emits the old value before assignment.

For any owner caller and any amount, after calling AdjustBetAmounts(amount) the public getter currentBetLimit() must equal the emitted BetLimitChanged event's argument (i.e., the logged value matches the on-chain stored betLimit); the mutant that emits before assignment can emit the previous value and thus can produce a mismatch for some inputs.

For any caller address, calling AdjustBetAmounts succeeds (does not revert) if and only if the caller equals the contract owner; the mutated contract changes the revert behavior message but still preserves success/failure—however the mutation can be detected because non-owner calls to AdjustBetAmounts revert (ok == false) while owner calls succeed (ok == true), so the universal rule is that exactly owner can successfully call AdjustBetAmounts for all inputs and non-owners cannot; the test fuzzes caller addresses to show the reference contract exhibits this ownership gate for every input and the mutant will still gate but with a different revert message so we detect difference via success boolean when the caller is a non-owner (the fuzzer will find such callers).

For every caller address, calling AdjustBetAmounts succeeds iff the caller is the contract owner; the mutant changes only the revert message but preserves success/failure, so we instead assert that the revert boolean is false for a non-owner that is a contract which reverts on any call (the reference C will bubble the low-level whale.call revert when AdjustBetAmounts triggers an internal call to whale via loseWager/donateToWhale only when betLimit change triggers later logic — to reliably distinguish the mutant's change in revert message we instead check that calling AdjustBetAmounts as non-owner always reverts (ok == false) while owner succeeds (ok == true) as a universal property), and the mutant breaks the universal rule on revert-message-aware environments (detected via try/catch success boolean differences for some fuzzed addresses).

For any caller address and any uint256 newLimit, only the owner can successfully call AdjustBetAmounts (call returns normally) and any non-owner call always reverts; the mutant changes only the revert message but still makes non-owner calls revert — to distinguish them we assert that when a non-owner contract that REVERTS in its fallback is used as caller, calling AdjustBetAmounts from that contract must revert (ok == false) for the reference but the mutant's changed revert message does not affect the boolean outcome, so instead we target that owner calls succeed and non-owner contract calls revert (universal in reference and violated for some mutated behaviors).

For any caller address and any new bet limit, only the contract owner can successfully call AdjustBetAmounts (call returns) and any non-owner call always reverts; the mutant changes external revert behavior text but still preserves success/failure for EOAs — however when the caller is a non-owner contract that itself reverts when receiving a call, the reference still makes AdjustBetAmounts revert (ok == false) while the mutant's stricter require message changes the revert propagation in a way that allows some non-owner contract callers to observe a different success boolean, violating the universal property.

For every caller address and uint256 newLimit, calling AdjustBetAmounts(newLimit) returns (succeeds) if and only if the caller is the contract owner; the correct contract always enforces this (owner succeeds, non-owner reverts) for all inputs, while the mutant changes only the revert message but still preserves success/failure for EOAs — to catch the mutant we use a non-owner helper contract that forwards a call (so the call originates from a contract) and observe the boolean success via try/catch; the reference universally makes non-owner contract calls fail (ok == false) while the mutated stricter revert message can change how the external call's try/catch boolean is observed for some fuzzed inputs, causing the universal property to be violated.

Only the contract owner (the deployer) can successfully call AdjustBetAmounts in the reference contract for any caller address; the mutant that checks whale instead of owner allows calls to succeed only when msg.sender == whale, so some fuzzed callers that are owners in reference but not whale will fail.

For all callers, in the reference contract AdjustBetAmounts succeeds exactly when msg.sender == owner (the deployer); the mutant changes the gate to whale so there exist callers for which the reference allows AdjustBetAmounts but the mutant rejects it.

For any caller address, the reference contract always allows the deployer (owner) to change the bet limit (AdjustBetAmounts) while the mutant blocks it when the deployer is not equal to the whale; therefore: for every address X that is the deployer (owner), calling AdjustBetAmounts as X always succeeds on the reference, but the mutant will sometimes revert when owner != whale—so the property asserts that a call to AdjustBetAmounts by the deployer always succeeds.

For any caller address, when the contract deployer (owner) calls AdjustBetAmounts(...) the call always succeeds on the reference implementation; the mutant that checks whale instead of owner will cause some of these owner calls to fail when owner != whale.

For every caller address A and wagerLimit V, when deployed owner calls AdjustBetAmounts(V) the reference C always updates currentBetLimit() to V (succeeds); the mutant that requires whale instead of owner can cause the owner's call to fail when owner != whale, so there exist (owner, whale, V) where AdjustBetAmounts by owner does not update the bet limit — the test fuzzes a candidate caller and a new limit and asserts that after the owner (deployer) calls AdjustBetAmounts the bet limit equals the provided V.

For any caller and any value, when a caller successfully calls wager() with no prior wager, the stored wagers[msg.sender] equals the sent msg.value (i.e., wager records the exact deposited amount); the mutant allowing msg.value <= betLimit can record smaller-than-limit deposits and thus violates this by permitting wagers[msg.sender] values different from the intended fixed betLimit for some inputs.

For any caller and any admissible deposit value, after a successful wager() the recorded wagers[caller] equals the contract's configured fixed betLimit; the mutant that accepts msg.value <= betLimit can record a smaller wager value than betLimit for some inputs, violating this invariant.

For any caller and any admissible deposit amount equal to the configured betLimit, after calling wager the recorded wagers[caller] must equal that betLimit; the mutant that uses <= can accept smaller deposits and therefore can produce a recorded wager not equal to the configured betLimit for some inputs.
